summary: Team Optimus developed Earth Jukebox, a web app that lets people hear NASA Earth data instead of only seeing it. Its Global Data Explorer lets users choose any place on a globe, load a year of NASA POWER data such as temperature, rainfall or wind, and listen as each month’s average becomes a musical note. Its EIC Jukebox plays NASA’s “Change in Night Lights 2012-2023” visualization while the app measures the brightness of video frames and turns it into live notes, with brighter frames giving higher pitch. This addresses the challenge by turning Earth information into a multisensory experience, with sound generated from real data rather than a recorded or AI-made soundtrack. The app is also built for accessibility, with keyboard controls, spoken descriptions, narration, optional voice commands, and downloadable data. It matters because maps and charts leave out blind and low-vision users and can hide patterns that the ear catches easily. Sonification makes environmental change more inclusive, engaging and memorable, and invites people to explore their own part of a changing planet. The team notes that the sound shows visual patterns and is not a calibrated scientific measurement.
details:
What it does and how it works: Earth Jukebox is a web app that turns NASA Earth data into sound. In the Global Data Explorer, users pick a place on a globe or search for one, load a year of daily NASA POWER data (temperature, humidity, precipitation, wind, surface pressure or solar radiation), and play it back so each month’s average becomes a musical note, with higher values giving higher pitch. In the EIC Jukebox, users watch NASA’s “Change in Night Lights 2012-2023” visualization (SVS 5313) while the app samples video frames, measures their brightness and maps it to notes on a pentatonic scale. The sound is synthesized live in the browser, not recorded or AI-generated.

Benefits and intended impact: The project makes Earth science accessible to people who cannot rely on maps and charts, including blind and low-vision users, and helps everyone notice patterns the ear catches more easily than the eye. We hope it makes environmental change more engaging and memorable, and encourages people to explore data about their own part of the world.

Tools: We built it as a web app with HTML, JavaScript and the Web Audio API for sound, using the NASA POWER API for place-based data and NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio and Earth Information Center for the visualization. It runs in a standard browser and is hosted on GitHub Pages, so no special hardware is needed.

Creativity: Instead of showing data, we let people play it as music, and combine a personal “choose your place” experience with an official NASA visualization.

Factors we considered: We prioritized accessibility with keyboard controls, spoken descriptions, narration, optional voice commands, a visible sound legend, a data table and downloadable CSV. We also credit NASA clearly, state that this is an independent student project, and are honest that brightness-based sound shows visual patterns rather than calibrated measurements.
